html:
On 6 February 1819 Stamford Raffles of the British East India Company signed a treaty with local Malay rulers that let the company set up a trading post on Singapore island. The date is counted as the founding of modern Singapore.

The island had been a port before. In the 14th century it was the trading town of Temasek, or Singapura, whose prince Parameswara went on to found the Malacca Sultanate. By 1819 it was home to a small Malay and Orang Laut population under the Johor Sultanate.

Raffles wanted a British base on the Strait of Malacca to break the Dutch grip on the region's trade. To get a legal grant, he recognised Hussein Shah, the elder brother passed over for the throne of Johor, as sultan, and signed with him and the local chief, the Temenggong. William Farquhar was left in charge of the new settlement.

Raffles made it a free port, with no duties on trade, and it grew fast as ships from China, India and the archipelago came to avoid Dutch taxes. The Dutch protested, but the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 left Singapore British. In 1826 it was joined with Penang and Malacca as the Straits Settlements.

Singapore has marked the founding with celebrations every fifty years, most recently in 2019. Its meaning is now debated: some see a colonial beginning, others the start of the city that, after independence in 1965, Lee Kuan Yew built into one of the richest states in Asia.
sum: On 6 February 1819 Stamford Raffles of the British East India Company signed a treaty with local Malay rulers that let the company set up a trading post on Singapore island. The date is counted as the founding of modern Singapore.
